analysis.one_liner: Applies borrowers' home-state interest rate caps to online payday loans and bans selling their financial data.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by six Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAFE Lending Act targeted high-cost online payday lenders. It would require any small loan of $5,000 or less made over the internet, phone, or mail to follow the interest rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing loopholes that let lenders charge triple-digit rates in states that ban them by operating offshore or through bank partners. It would also stop companies that sell loan applicants' Social Security and bank account numbers unless they actually make the loan, protect bank accounts from checks written without the customer's written approval, and give the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau power to shut down websites that break consumer lending laws. The bill was introduced on January 29, 2013, sent to the Banking Committee that same day, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who take out small online loans and currently face annual percentage rates of several hundred percent in states that cap rates, plus anyone whose bank account is drained by a remotely created check they never approved or whose loan application data is resold to strangers. Consumers would gain the right to dispute one-time electronic repayments the same way they can dispute recurring ones.

how_it_helps.text: Any small-dollar consumer loan of $5,000 or less made over the internet, phone, fax, or mail, or by a national bank, must comply with the annual percentage rate, interest, and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, closing the offshore-hosting and rent-a-bank loopholes.

A one-time electronic repayment of a small-dollar loan is treated as a preauthorized transfer, so borrowers get the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's error-resolution and dispute protections, and remotely created checks can only be issued by someone the consumer designated in writing, revocable at any time.

No one may broker, arrange, gather applications for, or distribute sensitive financial information like Social Security and bank account numbers in connection with a small-dollar loan unless that person is directly making the loan to the consumer.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau can investigate and issue cease-and-desist orders against offshore and onshore websites that violate federal, state, or tribal consumer financial law, and state attorneys general and tribes can file complaints that trigger orders requiring payment processors to block transactions with the offending site.
The Government Accountability Office must study the availability of capital on Indian reservations and the impact of small-dollar lending on tribal members' economic opportunity.

analysis.who_pays: Online payday and installment lenders, the lead-generation companies that profit from selling loan applications, banks that rent out their charters so lenders can evade state rate caps, and payment processors that would face orders to block transactions with rule-breaking sites.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online payday lenders and lead generators

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate a source of fast credit that some borrowers with poor credit use by choice; people shut out of bank loans could be pushed toward worse options if legal small-dollar lenders cannot operate profitably under state rate caps.

Enforcement against offshore lenders is difficult even with the new cease-and-desist tools, since sites can move to new domain names and jurisdictions outside the reach of U.S. courts, and the bill's own text acknowledges this by requiring a process for reconstituted sites.
The restrictions on remotely created checks and lead generation impose new compliance costs on payment processors and financial institutions, which can be passed on to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and direct: borrowers in states that cap interest rates would no longer be charged several hundred percent annual rates by lenders hiding offshore or behind bank partners, and they would gain real dispute rights over account withdrawals. The main cost is real but narrower: some borrowers who rely on these loans when banks will not lend them money could lose access and face worse alternatives. On balance, the bill's protections match what state legislatures have already decided their own residents should have; it extends those decisions across state lines rather than overriding them.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee never took the bill up after it was referred on introduction day, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 29, 2013, and read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote appear in the complete action history.

The bill's support was entirely Democratic: Senator Jeff Merkley sponsored it with Senators Tom Udall of New Mexico, Dick Durbin, and Richard Blumenthal as original cosponsors, joined by five Democratic cosponsors in total.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online payday lenders, lead generators, and their bank and payment-processing partners benefited, because they kept operating under the status quo, free to charge rates above what borrowers' home states allow and to sell applicants' financial data. Borrowers kept paying the same high-cost loans the bill would have restricted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online payday lenders and data brokers

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the SAFE Lending Act and recruited Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Tom Udall, Dick Durbin, and Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled in the two years before Congress ended.

against.name: Online payday lending industry
against.role: Lenders, lead generators, and allied payment and bank partners
against.what_they_did: The industry had a direct financial stake in blocking any extension of state rate caps to internet lending and pressed against such measures.

sides.party_line_note: All six Senate supporters were Democrats and no Republican cosponsor is recorded; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll call shows how anyone would have voted.

industries.industry: Online payday and small-dollar installment lenders
industries.note: These lenders profit by charging triple-digit annual rates to borrowers in states that ban such rates, using offshore hosting, tribal affiliations, or national bank partners to dodge state law. The bill would make the borrower's home-state rate cap apply everywhere, which is precisely the revenue it targets.

industries.industry: Lead generators and sellers of consumer financial data
industries.note: These firms make money collecting and reselling loan applicants' Social Security and bank account numbers without lending anything themselves. The bill bans that business outright unless the firm is the actual lender.

industries.industry: Banks that rent their charters to high-cost lenders
industries.note: Some banks earn fees by originating loans on behalf of payday lenders so the loans escape state rate caps. The bill closes that route by requiring national banks to follow the borrower's home-state rate law.

Processors would face a duty to block transactions with sites under cease-and-desist orders, but the bill pairs that duty with broad immunity from lawsuits for good-faith compliance, limiting their downside.

Tribal-affiliated lenders that profit from internet loans outside state caps would lose that revenue, but the bill also gives tribes standing to file complaints against offshore sites that harm their members and directs a GAO study of capital access on reservations.
